title: From a receipt to small functions
goal: Separate input, validation, calculation and output, then test functions with intermediate results.

prerequisites.text: You can describe control flow in a diagram.
Arithmetic is enough; function syntax is explained through examples.

sections.title: Start with the result the user needs
paragraphs: An order calculator can be described as: read input → validate → calculate → report. Instead of writing one long main, state the responsibility of each stage.
At a lower level, calculation splits into a subtotal and a discount operation. Validation enforces nonnegative values and a percentage between 0 and 100.
The receipt needs one final amount. Start there and ask which values are needed just before printing. A discounted total needs a subtotal and a rate, and a subtotal needs price and quantity.

diagram.caption: Top level of main
diagram.text:
read → validate → calculate → print
                     │
                     └─ subtotal → discountPrice

sections.title: Define contracts before implementation details
paragraphs: subtotal(price,qty) computes a total under an explicit valid-input assumption. valid returns true or false for the specified bounds.
Choose names that express purpose: subtotal is more helpful than doStuff. A reporting function need not know the internals of the calculation.
Calling valid answers only whether the inputs are allowed. For price 120 and quantity 3 it returns true. The value 360 comes from subtotal.

sections.title: Separate calculation from interaction
paragraphs: std::cin and std::cout belong at the application boundary. Computation functions should ideally not be tied to console interaction so the same logic can serve a UI or test.
valid and subtotal can then be examined independently. This reduces diagnostic complexity without replacing end-to-end tests.

To check subtotal on its own, give it two arguments and compare its return value. To check the whole program, supply stdin and compare stdout. The first narrows down a defect; the second checks the wiring.

sections.title: Manage dependencies
paragraphs: Higher-level orchestration calls lower-level functions. When each component receives only necessary arguments, changes are more localized and tests become focused.
In the example, main handles user input but subtotal does not. This separation is a reusable architecture principle.
Do not pass the percentage to subtotal because that function does not calculate a discount. When the rounding policy changes, revisit discountPrice and its tests.

sections.title: Diagnose a multi-step calculation
paragraphs: If a total is wrong, check input validation, intermediate subtotal and discount calculation in sequence. Each boundary has observable values.
For teaching we use int; professional monetary systems need explicit units, overflow policies and rounding conventions. Those are later topics in the curriculum.
If the output is not 270, check valid, subtotal=300 and saving=30 in order. Each matching intermediate value narrows the search for the cause.

sections.title: Reading a function call
paragraphs: A receipt for three items at 100 each with a 10% discount needs one amount. Follow the input through each intermediate value.
Predict the output. If the total were wrong, which step would you inspect first?

reveal.title: Compare your prediction and trace the steps
paragraphs: bool valid(...) declares a check returning true or false. Parameters receive argument values on a call; return supplies a result to the caller. In discountPrice(subtotal(price, qty), discount), the subtotal is needed first: 100 and 3 give 300, then a 10 percent discount gives 300 − 30 = 270. This data dependency does not require compressing all work into one line. Store the subtotal in a named variable while debugging.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: Price and quantity are integers 0..1000; discount is 0..100. Round the saving down to whole units: total = subtotal − (subtotal·discount)/100. The bounds keep intermediate products within a 32-bit int.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

sections.title: Try a separate task
paragraphs: Build a detailed receipt for price 37, quantity 3 and discount 15%. Print three space-separated numbers: subtotal, saving in whole units and total due. Implement valid, subtotal and discountPrice separately. Price and quantity are integers 0..1000, discount is 0..100. Round down the saving before subtraction. Print invalid on failed extraction or range checks.
Predict the first case and one boundary case. Practice has a separate starter. After running it, explain which check or operation produced each result.

selfcheck.prompt: The price is 100, the quantity is 3 and the discount is 100%. What does this source print?
feedback: Yes. The allowed saving equals the entire subtotal.
300 is the subtotal. The saving is then subtracted.

execution.label: predict

selfcheck.prompt: Why separate a pure calculation from I/O?
options: It becomes easier to test and reuse
It hides it from the compiler
selfcheck.feedback: Computation then remains independent of the user interface.
Its contract is about valid arguments.

options: Small functions with explicit roles and contracts

selfcheck.prompt: For input 37 3 15, write down the subtotal, the saving, and the amount due. A learner got the incorrect total 94. At which step could the extra rounding have happened?
selfcheck.feedback: The subtotal is 111. Round the saving down: 111 × 15 / 100 = 16. Subtracting gives 95. If you round down the amount due instead, 111 × 85 / 100 gives 94.

practice.title: Discounted receipt
practice.task: Build a detailed receipt for price 37, quantity 3 and discount 15%. Print three space-separated numbers: subtotal, saving in whole units and total due. Implement valid, subtotal and discountPrice separately. Price and quantity are integers 0..1000, discount is 0..100. Round down the saving before subtraction. Print invalid on failed extraction or range checks.
criteria: Each function receives only the data needed for its step.
Check the result of discountPrice separately, then verify all three receipt fields for 37 3 15.
Explain where 16 comes from and why saving plus the amount due reconstructs the subtotal.
practice.hint: The difference between subtotal and the amount due gives the saving in whole units.

steps.action: State the contracts of the three functions.
Connect the functions in main and check all three fields at the endpoint rates.

terms.definition: Breaking a large problem into smaller problems with explicit boundaries.
A named operation that receives arguments and can return a result.
The expected inputs, outputs and valid calling conditions.
How closely a component's responsibilities belong together.
